\subsection{Balanced growth, the wage share, and accumulation cycles}

All results in this subsection are for the cross-dual model of
Section~3.6 on synthetic economies, generated by
\texttt{paper/accumulation\_bifurcation.jl}. The reference economy has
\AccN{} sectors and capital mobility $\mu=\AccMu$. Along its balanced-growth
ray, the level system of Equation~\eqref{eq:crossdual} grows at the
predicted $g^\star=\AccGrowthRef\%$ (relative error \AccGrowthSimErr{}
over a simulation of 30 periods), and the TSSI and simultaneist profit
rates of Section~3.4 coincide to within \AccTssiGap: on a balanced-growth
path the per-unit data are constant, so the TSSI price map sits at its
simultaneist fixed point.

\emph{Distribution.} With variable-capital mobility switched off
($\mu_v=0$) and the default price-adjustment speed $\beta=\AccBetaDefault$,
balanced growth is locally stable at every one of \AccWageNPoints{}
points of the two wage-share sweeps (uniform $\omega\in[\AccWageOmegaMin,\AccWageOmegaMax]$, and
proportional scaling of the sectoral rates of exploitation, reaching
$\omega\in[\AccPropOmegaMin,\AccPropOmegaMax]$). The leading eigenvalue's real part stays between
\AccWageReMin{} and \AccWageReMax. The growth rate falls from
\AccWageGMax\% to \AccWageGMin\% and the aggregate profit rate from
\AccWageRMax\% to \AccWageRMin\% as $\omega$ rises; the top of that
range corresponds to implausibly low wage shares and serves only to
show the shape of the relation. The aggregate organic composition falls
from \AccWageKMax{} to \AccWageKMin. The two sweeps fall on the same
$g^\star(\omega)$ and $r^\star(\omega)$ curves (Figure~\ref{fig:wage},
left): in this model, distribution enters balanced growth essentially
through the aggregate wage share alone, not its sectoral pattern. The
ratio $g^\star/r^\star$ declines from \AccWageGoverRHi{} to \AccWageGoverRLo{} across the sweep, a
Cambridge-type relation whose effective saving rate falls as depreciation
weighs more. The approach to balanced growth is oscillatory (the leading
eigenvalue is complex) except for $\omega\ge\AccWageMonotoneFrom$.

\emph{Hopf bifurcation in $\mu_v$.} With slower price adjustment,
$\beta=\AccBetaHopf$, balanced growth is stable at $\mu_v=0$ (leading real
part \AccRealPartStart) and loses stability at $\mu_v=\AccMuvH$, where a
complex pair crosses the imaginary axis with speed
$\operatorname{Re}a=\AccHopfTransv$ and frequency \AccHopfOmega{} (period
\AccHopfPeriod). The first Lyapunov coefficient is $\ell_1=\AccHopfLyap<0$: the
bifurcation is supercritical, and a small stable accumulation cycle is
born. The continuation finds \AccNHopf{} Hopf points on the
equilibrium branch, the last at $\mu_v=\AccHopfLast$; only the first
changes the stability of balanced growth, the others add further
unstable directions. Figure~\ref{fig:cycles} shows the stability of
balanced growth and the branch of limit cycles continued from the first
Hopf point. The cycle grows quickly in amplitude (measured as the largest
swing of any sector's share of total capital) and stays stable up to a
Neimark--Sacker bifurcation at $\mu_v=\AccNSFirst$, where it gives way to
an invariant torus. The branch then turns back at
$\mu_v\approx\AccFoldUpper$ and forward again at a fold of cycles at
$\mu_v=\AccFoldList$; shortly after, the cycle, now of shorter period,
regains stability. The upper turning point is not flagged by the
Floquet-based detector at the continuation step used, a reminder that
bifurcations along the cycle branch are step-dependent.
Further Neimark--Sacker points (at $\mu_v=$ \AccNSFurther) and a period
doubling at $\mu_v=\AccPDFirst$ follow. By $\mu_v=2.5$ the cycle has
period \AccCyclePeriodEnd{} and amplitude \AccCycleAmpEnd, and the smallest
sector share along it falls to \AccCycleQminEnd: the oscillation nearly
wipes out sectors in turn, an economically implausible feature that we
return to below and in Section~6.2.

Direct simulation on a grid of \AccSimNGrid{} values of $\mu_v$ confirms
this picture (diamonds in Figure~\ref{fig:cycles}, right). Simulations
converge to balanced growth below the Hopf point. They settle on a
periodic orbit in \AccSimNPeriodic{} cases, \AccSimNMatched{} of which lie
on a stable part of the continued branch, with periods within
\AccSimPeriodDev\% and amplitudes within \AccSimAmpDev\% of the
collocation values (for example, period \AccSimPeriodOneOne{} at
$\mu_v=1.1$). The remaining periodic case ($\mu_v=$ \AccSimUnmatched,
period \AccSimUnmatchedPeriod) lies where the continued cycle is
unstable; we read it as phase locking on the torus rather than as a
point of the branch. The \AccSimNIrregular{} irregular cases ---
quasi-periodic between the first Neimark--Sacker point and the fold, and
irregular from $\mu_v\approx1.9$ --- are exactly where the continued
cycle is unstable.

\emph{Coexistence and chaos.} The fold of cycles implies that a stable
cycle and the torus may coexist. Sweeping $\mu_v$ up and then down by
simulation in steps of \AccHystStep{} confirms it
(Figure~\ref{fig:chaos}, right). For $\mu_v\in[\AccHystLo,\AccHystHi]$
the economy ends on the torus (mean amplitude \AccHystTorusAmp) when
$\mu_v$ is raised and on a stable cycle (mean amplitude
\AccHystCycleAmp, period \AccHystCyclePeriodHi{} falling to
\AccHystCyclePeriodLo) when it is lowered: which accumulation regime
prevails depends on the path by which mobility reached its current value.
The lower edge of the window is the fold of cycles; the upper edge is not
the branch's turning point at $\mu_v\approx\AccFoldUpper$ but the
destruction of the torus, between $\mu_v=\AccHystHi$ and \AccHystNext.

The three largest Lyapunov exponents, estimated over \AccLyapT{} time
units after a transient (Figure~\ref{fig:chaos}, left), separate the
regimes. The control cases come out as theory requires: on the stable
cycle at $\mu_v=1.1$, $|\lambda_1|=\AccLyapCycle$ and
$\lambda_2=\AccLyapCycleTwo$; on the torus at $\mu_v=1.3$, two exponents
vanish ($|\lambda_1|=\AccLyapTorusOne$, $|\lambda_2|=\AccLyapTorusTwo$)
and $\lambda_3=\AccLyapTorusThree$. Beyond the second Neimark--Sacker
point the largest exponent is positive at $\mu_v=$ \AccLyapChaosList{}
($\lambda_1$ between \AccLyapOneMin{} and \AccLyapOneMax{}), and it
agrees within \AccLyapICDev\% between the default and a randomly
perturbed initial condition. At $\mu_v=$ \AccLyapWindowMuv{} it is zero
to within \AccLyapWindowOne, a periodic window corresponding to the
phase-locked orbit found above. At $\mu_v=$ \AccHyperList{} a second
exponent is also positive (between \AccHyperTwoMin{} and
\AccHyperTwoMax{} across both initial conditions), the signature of
hyperchaos. The irregular regime is therefore chaotic, by the standard
numerical criterion. This is evidence, not proof: the exponents are
finite-time estimates, and the chaotic trajectories, like the cycles, come
close to the boundary of the simplex (smallest sector share
\AccLyapQuotaMin).

\emph{Hopf boundary.} Repeating the continuation for uniform wage shares
$\omega\in[\AccHopfCurveOmegaMin,\AccHopfCurveOmegaMax]$ traces the Hopf
boundary $\mu_{v,H}(\omega)$ (Figure~\ref{fig:wage}, right). The boundary
is supercritical throughout and rises with the wage share, from
\AccHopfCurveMuvMin{} to \AccHopfCurveMuvMax: a higher wage share makes
balanced growth more robust to variable-capital mobility. Between
$\omega=\AccHopfFreqJumpLo$ and $\AccHopfFreqJumpHi$ the frequency at the
boundary jumps from \AccHopfFreqBefore{} to \AccHopfFreqAfter: a different
eigenvalue pair becomes the first to cross, so a double-Hopf point lies
in that interval. Faster price adjustment is strongly stabilizing: for
$\beta\in\{\AccBetaList\}$ the first Hopf point lies at $\mu_v=$
\AccBetaMuvHList{} respectively.

\emph{Robustness.} In \AccRobN{} random economies with
$N=\AccRobNMin$--$\AccRobNMax$ sectors and $\beta=\AccBetaHopf$, balanced
growth at $\mu_v=0$ is stable in \AccRobNStable, loses stability at a Hopf
point in $\mu_v\in[0,4]$ in \AccRobNHopf, and that first Hopf point is
supercritical in \AccRobNSuper. It lies between $\mu_v=\AccRobMuvHMin$ and
\AccRobMuvHMax{} (median \AccRobMuvHMedian), with periods of the
bifurcating cycle between \AccRobPeriodMin{} and \AccRobPeriodMax; no
sector share on the equilibrium branches falls below \AccRobQuotaMin. The
supercritical Hopf bifurcation to accumulation cycles is therefore
generic in this class of economies, not a feature of the reference
example.

\emph{Exit friction.} The near-extinction of sectors along the cycles
suggests a missing brake: in the model, capital leaves a shrinking sector
as easily as a large one. An optional exit friction $\varepsilon\ge0$
damps each outflow of the mobility terms ($r_i<\bar r$) by
$s_i/(s_i+\varepsilon)$, with $s_i=C_i/\sum_jC_j$ the sector's share
($V$ shares for the $\mu_v$ term), and scales all inflows by a common
factor so that the term still sums to exactly zero. Shares are
scale-free, so the system stays homogeneous of degree~1 and balanced
growth is still a fixed point of the normalized flow. The default is
$\varepsilon=0$, and every other result in this section uses it.
Table~\ref{tab:exit-friction} repeats the direct simulations with
friction. At $\mu_v=\AccExitMuvMax$ the smallest sector share rises from
\AccExitShareOff{} without friction to \AccExitShareOn{} with
$\varepsilon=\AccExitEpsMax$. The friction is not neutral for the cycles
themselves: it changes which regime prevails at a given $\mu_v$, and at
$\mu_v=1.2$ the cycle amplitude falls from \AccExitAmpOffLow{} to
\AccExitAmpOnLow{} with $\varepsilon=\AccExitEpsMax$, so the Hopf point
moves up. Friction keeps sectors away from extinction, but it does not
remove the cycles at high $\mu_v$.

\subsection{Real final demand in the dynamics}

The final-use columns of the symmetric input-output table
(\texttt{NAIO\_10\_CP1700}, domestic use) give, for each product, how
much domestic output goes to household and NPISH consumption, government
consumption, capital formation and exports. MarxKapital reads them
alongside the technical matrix and sums them to the calibration's
sectors. Final demand is additive, so plain sums suffice, unlike the
Leontief aggregation of $A$. They enter the dynamics in two optional ways,
both run here on the 2022 Portuguese calibration with its real $A$
(Table~\ref{tab:final-demand}).

\emph{Rationing net of final demand.} Let $\varphi_i$ be the share of
sector $i$'s output that the table allocates to final consumption and
exports, $\varphi_i=(P3_i+P6_i)/TU_i$; capital formation is left out,
because the rationing mechanism models investment demand itself. The
shares are unit-free, so they carry over to the model's value units. At
19 sectors they range from \FDPhiMin{} (sector \FDPhiMinSector) to
\FDPhiMax{} (sector \FDPhiMaxSector), with \FDPhiCapped{} sectors at the
cap of $0.95$. Rationing then compares investment demand $D_i$ with
$(1-\varphi_i)x_i$ instead of $x_i$. At 10 and 19 sectors most sectors are
already rationed with $O=x$, and the deduction leaves that share
unchanged but lowers accumulation: rationing binds harder in the same
sectors. At three sectors no sector is rationed either way.

\emph{A real consumption basket.} In the cross-dual model all wage and
capitalist consumption buys a fixed basket, by default the shares of
initial net output. Replacing it with each sector's share of household
final consumption keeps Walras' law (the basket is still a set of shares
summing to one) and moves the balanced-growth rate $g^\star$ up at 10
and 19 sectors, with almost no change at three sectors and no change in
the stability of the ray.

Both results carry the caveat of Section~3.3: Eurostat's matrix covers
domestic inputs only, so the gross output reconstructed from it leaves
out imported intermediate inputs.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{A stock-flow conflation and a valuation artifact}

A first pass at the raw AMECO series appears to show a profit rate rising
sharply for Portugal over 1996--2022, driven by an organic composition
that falls even as the rate of exploitation nearly triples. This is the
pattern we originally reported. It does not survive a closer look, and
tracing why it does not survive turned out to require finding two
separate defects, not one.

\emph{The first defect was in the model, not the data.} Gross output
throughout MarxKapital was computed as $O_i=C_i+V_i+S_i$ (Section~3.3),
adding a capital \emph{stock} to two annual \emph{flows}; the aggregate
AMECO calculation used the same conflation implicitly, deducting a flat
$10\%$ of the (constant-price) capital stock as ``depreciation'' from a
current-price surplus. External review of an earlier draft caught this.
It matters here specifically because the flat-depreciation term breaks
an algebraic identity that should otherwise hold for the quantity
actually reported. The rate of exploitation used throughout this paper
is net of consumption of fixed capital, $e^{\text{net}}=(Y-V-\text{CFC})/V$
(Section~4.3); if $Y$, $V$, and CFC are \emph{all} deflated by a common
price index, $e^{\text{net}}$ is invariant under that deflation --- the
common factor cancels from every term. The earlier, buggy version
deducted a flat $10\%$ of the (constant-price) capital stock in place of
CFC: an unscaled term that does \emph{not} move with the deflator
applied to $Y$ and $V$, so it breaks precisely the invariance
$e^{\text{net}}$ should have, and breaks it in a way that depends on how
much the deflator itself has moved --- which changes over 26 years of
cumulative inflation, producing not just a level shift between
conventions but a diverging \emph{trend}. This, not a genuine valuation
difference, is what generated the original $e:0.21\to0.61$ figure. (The
purely gross quantity $S^{\text{gross}}/V=(Y-V)/V$, which never involved
CFC at all, was never the source of the problem; it is trivially
invariant under any common deflator regardless of this bug, since no
unscaled term ever entered it.)

We fixed the underlying conflation directly (Section~3.1, Section~4.3):
output-facing formulas now use $\delta_iC_i$ (capital \emph{transferred}
in a period) rather than $C_i$ (capital \emph{advanced}, a stock), and
the aggregate calculation now uses AMECO's own consumption-of-fixed-capital
series (properly deflated alongside $Y$ and $V$) rather than an assumed
rate. The predicted consequence is
checkable, and we checked it directly rather than asserting it: with the
fix, $e^{\text{net}}$ is now \emph{exactly} identical between the unadjusted
and GDP-deflated conventions for every year in the 1996--2022 series,
for both Portugal and Spain (Section~5.2). This is not a small
improvement in agreement --- it is exact equality to floating-point
precision, which is what the algebra predicts once every term shares a
common deflation factor, and is the strongest kind
of internal-consistency check a reader could ask for: not ``the numbers
look more reasonable now,'' but ``the two conventions are now provably
required to agree, and they do.''

\emph{The second, genuine question is the one we originally set out to
answer:} does AMECO's capital stock (constant-price) versus wage and
output series (current-price) distort the measured profit rate once the
depreciation bug is out of the way? It does, but modestly. Portugal's
profit rate now ranges $7.9\%$--$15.1\%$ across three deflation
conventions over the full period (Section~5.2) --- rising mildly from
$7.9\%$ to $11.5\%$ unadjusted, declining mildly at the endpoints from
$12.6\%$ to $10.9\%$ (ranging $9.3$--$12.7\%$ across the full period)
under the GDP deflator, and from $15.0\%$ to $12.3\%$ at the endpoints
(ranging $9.3$--$15.1\%$) under an investment-goods deflator. We checked the investment-deflator variant
specifically because AMECO's capital stock is a chain-linked series built
from investment flows using an investment-specific price index
(\texttt{PIGT}), not the general GDP deflator (\texttt{PVGD}); the two
give different \emph{levels} but the same qualitative shape (mild
decline), evidence the residual sensitivity is not an artifact of which
deflator was picked. Applying the GDP-deflated convention to Spain
(Figure~\ref{fig:ptvses}) shows the same modest pattern: a profit rate
moving from $12.0\%$ to $9.1\%$ against $7.9\%$ to $9.6\%$ unadjusted. We
do not read either country's series as proof of a general tendential
pattern from a two-country, single-source comparison; national-accounts
profit-rate estimates remain sensitive to depreciation conventions and
sectoral composition, discussed further in Section~6.2. We also could
not find, and do not believe AMECO publishes, a current-price
(replacement-cost) capital-stock series that would let us skip deflation
entirely and compare all three quantities at a common current-year
valuation, which would be the cleanest check in principle.

We report the full sequence --- the original artifact, the stock-flow bug
that substantially manufactured it, the fix, and the smaller genuine
sensitivity that remains --- rather than only the corrected numbers,
because the sequence is the more durable methodological finding here: an
automated pipeline that conflates a stock with a flow, or mixes
valuation conventions across variables pulled from the same database,
can each independently manufacture a statistically salient but spurious
trend, and the two can compound. Disaggregating the corrected aggregate
trend by sector, and comparing it against the 2022 cross-section of
Table~\ref{tab:sectors}, is beyond the scope of this paper ---
complicated further by the single-year nature of the sectoral
calibration versus the time-series nature of the aggregate result ---
and is left for future work.

\subsection{Limitations}

We report limitations transparently, following the same practice as the
package's own documentation.

\emph{Default behavior remains synthetic.} Both calibration paths default
to synthetic data or fixed sectoral weights; every real-data result in
this paper required explicit opt-in flags. This is a deliberate design
choice to keep the package's automated test suite fully offline, not a
limitation of the real-data pipeline itself, but it means synthetic
results should never be mistaken for empirical ones when using the
package's defaults.

\emph{Single-rate depreciation.} The perpetual-inventory capital-stock
option (Section~4.3) uses one depreciation rate per sector, not
differentiated by asset type. Eurostat publishes investment by asset type
for the relevant dataflow, but not the corresponding asset-specific
depreciation profiles, which would be needed for a fully differentiated
perpetual-inventory calculation.

\emph{The dynamical model's output measure was resolved; final demand
was not.} An earlier version of this paper used a value-added-type flow
$W_i=\delta_iC_i+V_i+S_i$ as the supply side of Section~3.3's coupling
mechanisms, omitting circulating constant capital (materials, energy,
purchased services) entirely. We closed this gap rather than continuing
to disclose it: Equation~\eqref{eq:output-bruto} reconstructs genuine
gross output $x_i$ from $W_i$ and the model's own cost structure at
every solver evaluation, without adding new state, and both coupling
mechanisms now use $x_i$. The investment-demand side was fixed
correspondingly (Equation~\eqref{eq:rationing}): $A_{ij}$ now multiplies
a desired \emph{output} expansion $\Delta x_j$, converted from planned
investment expenditure via the sector's own capital-output ratio, not
raw expenditure directly. One gap remains, now partly closed: by
default the quantity-rationing mechanism treats the \emph{full}
reconstructed $x_i$ as available to meet investment demand, though
output must also replace intermediate inputs and meet consumption and
other final demand first. The input-output table's final-use columns now
allow the second deduction on real-data calibrations (Section~5.7):
netting final consumption and exports out of supply lowers accumulation
but does not change which sectors are rationed. Intermediate replacement
is still not netted, so even then $D_i\le(1-\varphi_i)x_i$ is an upper
bound on investable supply, not a fully netted reproduction balance.

\emph{Limited robustness and sensitivity analysis, partially addressed.}
We report the aggregate trend under three valuation conventions
(unadjusted, GDP-deflated, investment-deflated; Section~5.2 and
Section~6.1) and for two countries (Portugal and Spain), which is enough
to show the corrected finding is not a single-country, single-deflator
artifact, but not enough to establish a general pattern across
peripheral EU economies, nor to rule out sectoral composition effects
that an aggregate series cannot separate from a genuine average-rate
change. The sectoral profile (Table~\ref{tab:sectors}) still uses a
single set of choices: net capital stock rather than perpetual-inventory,
and a single value of the mobility coefficient $\mu$. For the coupling
mechanisms of Section~3.3, we no longer rely on a single random seed: a
270-trial sweep (Section~5.4) confirms the rationing fixed point
converges reliably ($270/270$) across varied $N$, matrix density, and
demand/supply configurations, and a 50-seed sweep confirms rationing
produces higher dispersion than mobility alone systematically
($50/50$ seeds), not as an artifact of one draw. What these sweeps do
not cover: a fixed $\mu$ and fixed relaxation parameter throughout, and
only random (not empirically calibrated) technical matrices for the
dynamic comparison, since no real per-sector accumulation series exists
to calibrate it against (Section~5.4). Section~3.3
establishes that a fixed point always exists (Brouwer), explains
structurally why undamped iteration oscillates rather than converges
(the map is antitone, and Proposition~\ref{prop:triangular} shows
undamped iteration sits exactly on a flip boundary whenever rationing
binds), gives direct empirical evidence of practical
uniqueness under variation in initial conditions, sector ordering, and
tolerance in one genuinely-rationed test case, and proves that damped
iteration converges locally, at a rate the exact spectrum predicts, for
every relaxation $\alpha\in(0,1)$ at every generic fixed point. What
remains open is a uniqueness \emph{proof} and a \emph{global}
convergence guarantee from arbitrary initial $\rho$ across all
admissible $(A,\sigma,S,O)$ --- and Section~3.3's
own negative result suggests the obvious route to the latter, a global
Lipschitz bound in the spirit of $\rho(A)<1$, cannot supply it: we
showed algebraically that its tightest admissible form always exceeds
$1$ whenever any sector is actually rationed. Closing this gap, if it
can be closed at all, likely requires a different technique --- possibly
exploiting the antitone structure directly (e.g.\ bounding $F\circ F$)
rather than a Banach-style argument on $F$ itself --- and we continue to
rely on the empirical evidence above for the general case in the
meantime.

\emph{The technical matrix construction was audited, and the audit found
a bigger problem than expected.} We set out to quantify a margin-clipping
step's effect, reconcile row/column totals, document the CPA-to-NACE
concordance, and resolve the domestic-vs-total-use question
(\texttt{paper/matrix\_audit.jl}). Instead we found the pipeline had been
pulling from the wrong Eurostat dataflow entirely (Section~4.2):
\texttt{NAIO\_10\_CP1620} is a trade-and-transport-margins satellite
table, not the symmetric input-output table, and building $A$ from it
understated intermediate flows by more than an order of magnitude ---
the direct cause of the implausibly low $\rho(A)\approx0.13$ and
implausibly high $R_{\max}\approx691\%$ this paper previously reported,
and of every negative cell we had attributed to a margin-accounting
convention. Rebuilt from the correct table (\texttt{NAIO\_10\_CP1700}),
the matrix has zero negative cells, reconciles \emph{exactly} against
the table's own published output row for all 19 sections, and gives
$\rho(A)\approx0.52$, $R_{\max}\approx91\%$ --- both economically
plausible. The domestic-vs-total-use question is also resolved rather
than left open: the correct table publishes a genuine domestic-use
variant, which we use, directly addressing the concern that imported
inputs were being modeled as domestic supply. The CPA-to-NACE
concordance question does not require a documented mapping \emph{inside}
the matrix construction step itself: the symmetric table's two
dimensions (\texttt{prd\_ava}, \texttt{prd\_use}) both use the same CPA
product code, so $A$ is built entirely within one classification, with
no product-to-industry join. A concordance assumption is still made one
level up, where $A$'s CPA-labeled sections are combined with
NACE-classified labor coefficients (\texttt{NAMA\_10\_A64}) for the
production-structure analysis of Figures~\ref{fig:matrixA}--\ref{fig:transformation}.
Table~\ref{tab:sectors} is constructed independently, directly from
NACE-classified sectoral accounts, and does not depend on $A$ at all
(Section~5.1). We rely on
Eurostat's standard design correspondence between CPA and NACE section
codes at this level of aggregation (both derive from the same top-level
classification structure) rather than an independently verified
concordance table, and label $A$'s axes as CPA product sections, not
NACE industry sections, to keep this distinction visible. What remains
unresolved, and cannot be fixed by writing more code:
\texttt{NAIO\_10\_CP1700} is a benchmark table published for specific
reference years (2010, 2013, 2015, 2017, 2020 for Portugal), not
annually. We resolved the resulting vintage question by scoping rather
than by leaving a silent mismatch: Figures~\ref{fig:matrixA}
and~\ref{fig:transformation} now use a fully coherent 2020 calibration
(matrix and labor coefficients both 2020), while Table~\ref{tab:sectors}
and the aggregate AMECO series remain genuinely 2022, since neither
depends on $A$. The paper's empirical results therefore span two
internally-coherent reference points rather than one section silently
mixing 2020 and 2022 data (Section~4.2). An
explicit accounting-reconciliation assertion in the pipeline (failing
loudly if a sector's computed output does not match the table's own
\texttt{P1} row, in the spirit of the GVA check in Section~5.1) would be
a reasonable next hardening step, though the reconciliation is already
exact in the cases we checked.

\emph{The mobility term's conservation was fixed} (Section~3.3): an
earlier draft's $\bar r$ did not guarantee $\sum_i\mu(r_i-\bar r)C_i=0$;
redefining $\bar r$ as the $C_i$-weighted mean of $r_i$ makes this hold
by construction, verified directly rather than assumed. \emph{The
rationing mechanism's demand term was also fixed}: an earlier draft
applied $A_{ij}$ directly to planned investment \emph{expenditure}
$\sigma_{c,j}S_j$, as if a unit of investment spending required the same
input mix as a unit of physical output. Section~3.3's
$\Delta x_j=\sigma_{c,j}S_j\cdot x_j/C_j$ resolves this by converting
expenditure to an output-scale quantity via the sector's own
capital-output ratio before $A_{ij}$ is applied to it. One simplification
remains: by default the full reconstructed $x_i$ is treated as available
for investment demand $D_i$ before intermediate replacement (already
counted in $z_i$) and consumption and other final demand are met,
overstating investable supply. Final consumption and exports can now be
netted out on real-data calibrations (Section~5.7); intermediate
replacement cannot, so $D_i\le x_i$ should still be read as an upper
bound on investable supply, not a fully netted reproduction balance
(Section~3.3).

\emph{The TSSI layer and the bifurcation analysis have a deliberately
narrow scope.} TSSI is implemented as a valuation of trajectories, not
as a driver of them: the mobility term of Section~3.3 still uses
simultaneist (Sraffian) profit rates, and a TSSI-driven variant of the
dynamics is not implemented. The production lag $\tau$ is a single
fixed constant, not a distribution of turnover times by sector.
Depreciation $d_j$ is valued at base prices by default; an optional
historical-cost variant keeps a book value of fixed capital per sector,
bought at lagged TSSI prices of each sector's capital good, and leaves
the invariants intact. The bifurcation analysis concerns the two maps of
Section~3.5; the accumulation ODEs themselves have no equilibria in
levels and would need rewriting in normalized variables (capital
shares, organic compositions) before their own bifurcations could be
studied. Hessians (\texttt{system\_hessian}) are available for the
ODE right-hand side but not through the rationing fixed point, whose
implicit-function derivative is first-order only.

\emph{The cross-dual extension and its cycles rest on strong, uncalibrated
assumptions.} Market prices adjust at a single speed $\beta$, final
demand is a fixed basket (initial net-output shares by default, or real
household consumption shares on real-data calibrations, Section~5.7),
and neither $\beta$ nor
the variable-capital mobility $\mu_v$ is estimated. The Hopf points and
cycles of Section~5.6 are therefore properties of the model class, not
claims about any economy. The cycles approach the boundary of the
simplex (sector shares of order $10^{-4}$), which points to a missing
braking mechanism. The optional exit friction of Section~5.6 is one such
mechanism; it raises the smallest shares most where they are smallest,
but its functional form and the size of $\varepsilon$ are
assumptions, not estimates, and entry of new capital is not modeled.
Numerically, two Hopf points within one continuation step escape
detection (we use a step of at most $0.01$ and check against a direct
count of unstable eigenvalues), and bifurcations along the cycle branch
depend on the step size, so we treat them as established only where
direct simulation agrees. The chaos claim rests on finite-time
Lyapunov exponents: they are robust to the initial condition, the
integration tolerance and the run length in our checks, but they are not
a computer-assisted proof.

\emph{Reproducibility is live-query reproducibility, not archival
reproducibility.} Every result in this paper is produced by re-running
\texttt{generate\_results.jl} against the live Eurostat and AMECO SDMX
APIs (Availability, below), which is re-runnable but not immune to
retroactive revisions in the underlying series, dataset vintages, or API
structure --- a live query today is not guaranteed to reproduce a number
reported here indefinitely. A stronger reproducibility architecture
would pair a tagged package release with cached raw API responses (or a
frozen archival snapshot, e.g.\ on Zenodo) alongside the live-query path,
letting a reader choose between reproducing this paper's exact reported
numbers from frozen data and refreshing the analysis against current
data; we have not built this yet.

\section{Conclusion}

MarxKapital demonstrates that a real, live, officially sourced data
pipeline for Marxian value-theoretic calibration is practical using
current European statistical infrastructure, and that an exact per-sector
quantity-rationing mechanism --- solving a genuine fixed point, though
not imposing hard market clearing at every instant (Section~3.3) --- can
be added to a reproduction-schema model without the numerical overhead
of a formal differential-algebraic formulation. Applied to Portugal and
Spain, the pipeline surfaces --- and lets us diagnose and fix --- two
distinct measurement problems: a stock-flow conflation in the model's
own output formula, caught by external review, and a resulting
valuation artifact in the aggregate profit-rate series that we had
originally overstated because of it. Corrected, the underlying trend is
real but modest --- a $7.9\%$--$15.1\%$ range for Portugal across three
deflation conventions, not the near-fivefold swing an earlier, buggy
version of this calibration reported. Two further defects surfaced by
the same review process are also fixed and verified directly rather than
merely asserted: the capital-mobility term now conserves aggregate
constant capital exactly by construction, and the rationing mechanism's
convergence and dispersion claims (Section~5.4) now rest on systematic
sweeps of 270 and 50 random economies respectively, not a single
hand-picked illustration. The exact Jacobian of the rationing map,
computed by automatic differentiation, turned the convergence claim
from a purely empirical one into a partly proved one: the Jacobian is
triangular, its spectrum lies in $[-1,0]$, damped iteration converges
locally for every $\alpha\in(0,1)$, and undamped iteration lies exactly
on a flip boundary that a continuation analysis locates at the
border-collision onset of rationing. A temporal single-system
valuation layer with fixed production lag shows TSSI prices converging
to simultaneist ones under frozen data in every economy tested. Rewriting
the accumulation dynamics in normalized variables shows that the
value-accounting model has no interior balanced growth; with market
prices that respond to excess demand it does, and that balanced growth
gives way to accumulation cycles through a supercritical Hopf
bifurcation in the mobility of variable capital, at a threshold that
rises with the wage share and with the speed of price adjustment; at
higher mobility the cycles give way to coexisting attractors and to
chaos. A fourth audit, of the technical matrix
itself, found the most serious defect of the four: the pipeline had been
using the wrong Eurostat dataflow, understating intermediate flows by
more than an order of magnitude and producing an implausible spectral
radius and maximum profit rate that this paper had, in an earlier
version, reported without knowing why they looked wrong. Rebuilt from
the correct table, the matrix reconciles exactly against its own
published output figures and gives economically plausible values
throughout (Section~4.2, Section~6.2). A fifth defect, in the dynamical
model itself, was resolved rather than only disclosed: the coupling
mechanisms' supply side omitted circulating constant capital entirely,
and their investment-demand side applied the technical matrix to
expenditure rather than output. Both are fixed by reconstructing genuine
gross output from the model's own state at every solver evaluation
(Section~3.1, Equation~\eqref{eq:output-bruto}) and converting planned
investment expenditure to an output-scale quantity via each sector's
capital-output ratio before applying $A$ to it (Section~3.3) --- neither
requires new state or a heavier solver. We think this exercise is itself a
useful illustration of what a live, multi-source statistical pipeline
buys a computational Marxian model: not just convenience, but the
ability to catch exactly this kind of measurement and modeling error
before it is mistaken for an economic finding --- provided the pipeline
is checked as carefully as the theory it implements, and provided
implausible intermediate results (a spectral radius an order of
magnitude too low, in this case) are investigated rather than reported
with a caveat and left for later. Extending the
valuation-consistent comparison to more economies and archiving frozen data
snapshots for stronger reproducibility guarantees (Section~6.2) are left
for future work.

\section*{Availability}

MarxKapital is released under the MIT license. The complete source code,
including the empirical pipeline described here, is available at
\url{https://github.com/randsley/MarxKapital}. Every figure and table in
this paper is produced, without manual editing, by
\texttt{paper/generate\_results.jl}, which performs live queries against
the Eurostat and AMECO SDMX APIs; re-running it reproduces this paper's
results from the same official data sources. The synthetic sweeps of
Sections~5.4--5.5 are produced offline by \texttt{paper/monte\_carlo.jl}
and \texttt{paper/jacobian\_bifurcation.jl}; the latter also writes every
number quoted in Sections~3.4 and~5.5 to
\texttt{paper/figures/jacobian\_stats.tex}, which the paper reads
directly.
